newsitem.title: USA: Suit won't stop bonds for Milwaukee stadium - lawyer.
newsitem.headline: Suit won't stop bonds for Milwaukee stadium - lawyer.

text.p: An attorney representing a government panel overseeing a new professional baseball stadium in Milwaukee said Monday that an appeal in a lawsuit filed by a group of taxpayers against a tax slated to support bonds for the project would not stop the sale of the bonds.

Jon Axelrod, who is representing the Southeast Wisconsin Professional Baseball Park District Board, said that he and other attorneys working for plaintiffs in the case would render an opinion that the lawsuit has no merit and is frivolous.

He said that opinion would be forwarded to Nelson Flynn, an attorney at Michael, Best & Fredrich, the bond counsel for $160 million of tax-exempt bonds the stadium board plans to issue for the stadium.

The lawsuit challenges the constitutionality of a 0.1 percent, five-county sales tax put into place by the Wisconsin Legislature to help finance a new $250 million stadium for the Milwaukee Brewers American League baseball team.

Patrick Born, a senior vice president at Evenson Dodge Inc, the financial advisor on the project, has said that the lawsuit could be an impediment to the bond sale unless it was resolved in the stadium board's favor.
On Monday, Born said it would be a "very rare" situation to sell bonds while a challenge to their payment stream is still pending.
However, if the bond sale proceeds, Born said the lawsuit would have to be carefully disclosed and discussions would have to be held with potential bond buyers.
"Even if the district wishes to proceed, they still need folks to buy the bonds," Born said.
Michael Duckett, executive director for the stadium board, said discussions were also being held with insurance companies on insuring the bonds.
Earlier this month, a federal court judge in Milwaukee dismissed the group's lawsuit on the grounds the Wisconsin Supreme Court had already ruled the sales tax was constitutional.

At a press conference Monday in Milwaukee, George Watts, one of the taxpayers who filed the lawsuit, said that the federal court judge's ruling would be appealed in the U.S. Appellate Court in Chicago.
He said the appeal would be made despite threats contained in a letter from Axelrod that said the stadium board would seek monetary sanctions against the group if they decide to appeal.

Axelrod defended his letter saying it was not a threat, but a means of "protecting taxpayers" who have paid more than $50,000 in attorney's fees to defend the stadium board in the fight over the sales tax.
"They are filing the same lawsuit over and over again," Axelrod said. "We don't think it's fair taxpayers should pay for that."
The stadium board is scheduled to vote on the bond resolution at its meeting next month.
